title: Docker images and containers
idea: An image is a read-only template built from layers. A container is a running instance of an image, with its own writable layer.

analogy.text: A class and its objects. The class is written once; each object is created from it and keeps its own state.
analogy.breaks: An image never changes after the build.

points: `docker build` turns a Dockerfile into an image made of read-only layers.
`docker run` creates a container from an image and starts it.
Each container adds its own thin writable layer on top.
One image can start many containers, and stopping them leaves the image untouched.

edges.label: docker build
edges.caption: `docker build` runs each Dockerfile line and stores the result as read-only layers in an image.

edges.label: docker run
edges.caption: `docker run` starts a container from the image and adds a writable layer on top.

edges.label: docker run
edges.caption: Run it again and you get a second container. Both share the same image layers.

code.caption: A shell session: build one image, start two containers from it, then stop one.

walk.text: Build an image from the Dockerfile here and tag it `shop:1`.
Start two detached containers from the same image. `--name` labels each one.
List running containers. Both appear, with the image they came from.
List images named `shop`. There is one, however many containers use it.
Stop `shop-a`. The container keeps existing; it just is not running.
`-a` lists stopped containers too. Without it, `shop-a` would not show.

pitfalls: Files written inside a container never change its image; rebuild the image to keep changes.
`docker rm` deletes a container's writable layer, and every file written there.
Run `docker ps -a` to find stopped containers; plain `docker ps` hides them.

quiz.q: You start three containers from one image. How many images exist?
options: Three, but only one is running
quiz.why: Containers are instances, not copies. They share the image's read-only layers and add only a writable layer each.

takeaway: Build an image once; start as many containers from it as you need.
